## 11.3 Valence, arousal, dominance and concreteness of the explanations

Each explanation is scored on four published word norms. Valence, arousal
and dominance come from Warriner, Kuperman and Brysbaert (2013), who
collected ratings of 13,915 English lemmas (dictionary forms of words) on 1
to 9 scales: valence from unhappy to happy, arousal from calm to excited,
dominance from controlled to in control. Concreteness comes from Brysbaert,
Warriner and Kuperman (2014), who collected ratings of 39,954 English words
and two-word expressions on a 1 to 5 scale from abstract to concrete. An
explanation's score on a norm is the mean of the norm over its content words
that have an entry. The rating questions' own words are removed first, so
"creative" and "effort" do not drive the score. A word with no exact entry
is tried once more with a final s, es, ed or ing removed. An explanation
with no matching word has no score. The norms were built by other
laboratories for other purposes, before this study existed. The files and
their checksums are recorded in `nlp/norms/README.md`.

```{r supp-table-text-affect-by-arm}
render_prereg_table(
  csv_name    = "study1_text_affect_by_arm.csv",
  tex_name    = "sup_table_text_affect_by_arm.tex",
  caption     = function(df) paste0(
    "Valence, arousal and dominance (Warriner, Kuperman and Brysbaert, 2013; ",
    "1 to 9 scales: unhappy to happy, calm to excited, controlled to in ",
    "control) and concreteness (Brysbaert, Warriner and Kuperman, 2014; 1 to ",
    "5, abstract to concrete) of the written explanations, by arm within each ",
    "rating dimension. An explanation's score is the mean norm over its ",
    "content words that have an entry, with the rating questions' own words ",
    "removed and one fallback match after a final s, es, ed or ing is ",
    "stripped; explanations with no matching word are left out. The scores ",
    "describe the words people chose after giving their rating and are not ",
    "measures of the artwork.",
    writer_quote(df, "model", "The analysis records the comparison as")),
  label       = "supp_text_affect_by_arm",
  pending_msg = paste0("run Study1_03_Integration.Rmd (word-norm scores of ",
                       "the explanations by arm, from ",
                       "nlp/study1_text_affect.csv, which ",
                       "Study1_02_Text.ipynb writes)"),
  transform   = drop_long_constant_columns,
  stage       = "integration"
)
```

## 11.4 Topics in the explanations

The explanations are also described without any word list chosen in
advance. A topic model finds, from the word counts alone, a small number of
word groups ("topics") such that each explanation is approximately a
weighted mix of them. The model here is non-negative matrix factorisation.
It writes the table of explanations by words as the product of two tables
with no negative entries. One gives each explanation's weight on each topic,
the other each topic's weight on each word. Each word is weighted by tf-idf,
its count in the explanation scaled down by how many explanations use it, so
common words count for less. The model is fitted separately to the
creativity and the effort explanations. It uses content words that appear in
at least five explanations, with the function words and the rating
questions' own words removed, and it never sees the condition or the rating.
Each explanation's topic weights are rescaled to sum to 1.

The number of topics is set by a rule fixed in the notebook. For each number
from 3 to 10, the model is refitted from ten random starting points.
Stability is the average, over every pair of starts, of how closely the
topics of one start match those of the other. Each topic of one start is
paired one-to-one with a topic of the other so that the total similarity is
as high as possible. Similarity is the cosine of the angle between the two
topics' word weights: 1 for identical word profiles, 0 for profiles with no
word in common. The number with the highest stability is used, the smaller
on a tie.

Three tables follow. The first gives that rule's numbers. The second gives
each topic's mean weight by arm, labelled by the topic's five heaviest
words. The third checks that the topics are not an artefact of counting
words. For that check, each explanation is turned into a vector of numbers
by a pretrained sentence-embedding model (all-mpnet-base-v2, run from a
local copy). That model is a network trained by others on large amounts of
text so that sentences of similar meaning get nearby vectors. The vectors are
grouped into the same number of clusters by k-means, a method that splits
them into that many groups so that each vector sits closer to the centre of
its own group than to any other. The adjusted Rand index then compares those
clusters with each explanation's heaviest topic. It measures agreement
between two groupings beyond what chance would produce: 0 is chance and 1 is
identical groupings. No measure or test in the paper rests on the embedding
model.

```{r supp-table-text-topics-stability}
# Column contract from the writer (Study1_02_Text.ipynb):
# dimension, k, stability_mean, stability_sd, chosen. One row per dimension
# and number of topics, k from 3 to 10.
render_prereg_table(
  csv_name    = "text_topics_stability.csv",
  tex_name    = "sup_table_text_topics_stability.tex",
  caption     = paste0(
    "How the number of topics was set, for the creativity and the effort ",
    "explanations separately. For each number of topics k from 3 to 10 the ",
    "topic model is refitted from ten random starting points; ",
    "stability\\_mean is the mean, over every pair of starts, of the average ",
    "cosine similarity between the word weights of topics paired one-to-one ",
    "across the two starts so that the total similarity is as high as ",
    "possible, and stability\\_sd its standard deviation over those pairs. ",
    "chosen marks the k with the highest stability, the smaller k on a tie, ",
    "which is the number of topics used."),
  label       = "supp_text_topics_stability",
  pending_msg = "run Study1_02_Text.ipynb (the topic model and its stability rule)",
  transform   = function(df) {
    if (all(c("dimension", "k") %in% names(df))) df <- arrange(df, dimension, k)
    df
  },
  stage       = "text"
)
```

```{r supp-table-text-topics-by-arm}
# Column contract: tables/text_topics_top_words.csv from the notebook carries
# dimension, topic, rank, word, weight, the ten heaviest words of each topic;
# tables/study1_text_topics_by_arm.csv from the integration file carries the
# topic weights by arm. Each topic is labelled here by its five heaviest
# words, joined on dimension and topic. Both are read as text, so a topic
# number matches whether it was written as a number or a string. When the
# word table is absent, or carries no row for a topic, the topic is rendered
# without a label and the console says so. The deposited CSVs are not
# changed.
topic_words <- read_table_or_null(
  "text_topics_top_words.csv",
  "run Study1_02_Text.ipynb (the topic model's top words)",
  stage = "text")

topic_labels <- if (!is.null(topic_words) &&
                    all(c("dimension", "topic", "rank", "word") %in% names(topic_words))) {
  topic_words %>%
    mutate(dimension = as.character(dimension),
           topic     = as.character(topic)) %>%
    filter(rank <= 5) %>%
    arrange(dimension, topic, rank) %>%
    group_by(dimension, topic) %>%
    summarise(top_words = paste(word, collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop")
} else NULL

add_topic_labels <- function(df) {
  if (is.null(topic_labels) || !all(c("dimension", "topic") %in% names(df))) {
    cat("Topics rendered without word labels (",
        if (is.null(topic_labels)) "no top-word table" else
          "no dimension and topic columns in the by-arm table", ").\n", sep = "")
    return(drop_long_constant_columns(df))
  }
  out <- df %>%
    mutate(dimension = as.character(dimension),
           topic     = as.character(topic)) %>%
    left_join(topic_labels, by = c("dimension", "topic")) %>%
    relocate(top_words, .after = topic)
  n_unlabelled <- sum(is.na(out$top_words))
  if (n_unlabelled > 0L) {
    cat(n_unlabelled, " row(s) of the by-arm table found no top-word label.\n",
        sep = "")
  }
  drop_long_constant_columns(out, keep = "top_words")
}

render_prereg_table(
  csv_name    = "study1_text_topics_by_arm.csv",
  tex_name    = "sup_table_text_topics_by_arm.tex",
  caption     = function(df) paste0(
    "Topics in the written explanations by arm, within each rating dimension. ",
    "Each topic is a group of words found by non-negative matrix ",
    "factorisation of the tf-idf weighted word counts, fitted to each ",
    "dimension's explanations without the condition or the rating, and is ",
    "labelled by its five heaviest words (top\\_words). An explanation's topic ",
    "weights sum to 1, so a topic's mean weight in an arm is the average share ",
    "of an explanation in that arm that the topic accounts for. The weights ",
    "describe what the explanations talk about; each explanation was written ",
    "after its rating, so a difference between arms is not a cause of the ",
    "rating difference.",
    writer_quote(df, "model", "The analysis records the comparison as")),
  label       = "supp_text_topics_by_arm",
  pending_msg = paste0("run Study1_03_Integration.Rmd (topic weights by arm, ",
                       "from nlp/study1_text_topics.csv, which ",
                       "Study1_02_Text.ipynb writes)"),
  transform   = add_topic_labels,
  stage       = "integration"
)
```

```{r supp-table-text-topics-embedding-agreement}
# Column contract from the writer (Study1_02_Text.ipynb): dimension, k, ari,
# and a note column when the embedding model could not be loaded from its
# local copy, in which case ari is NA. The note is kept in the typeset table
# even when it is one sentence on every row, since an NA ari cannot be read
# without it.
render_prereg_table(
  csv_name    = "text_topics_embedding_agreement.csv",
  tex_name    = "sup_table_text_topics_embedding_agreement.tex",
  caption     = paste0(
    "A check that the topics are not an artefact of counting words. Each ",
    "explanation is turned into a vector of numbers by a pretrained ",
    "sentence-embedding model (all-mpnet-base-v2, run from a local copy), a ",
    "network trained on large amounts of text so that sentences of similar ",
    "meaning get nearby vectors; the vectors are grouped into k clusters by ",
    "k-means, which splits them into k groups so that each vector sits closer ",
    "to the centre of its own group than to any other, k being the number of ",
    "topics chosen for that dimension; and ari is the adjusted Rand index ",
    "between those clusters and ",
    "each explanation's heaviest topic: the agreement between the two ",
    "groupings beyond what chance would produce, 0 for chance and 1 for ",
    "identical groupings. No measure or test in the paper rests on the ",
    "embedding model. An NA ari means the model could not be loaded from its ",
    "local copy, and the note column says so."),
  label       = "supp_text_topics_embedding_agreement",
  pending_msg = "run Study1_02_Text.ipynb (the embedding check on the topics)",
  transform   = function(df) drop_long_constant_columns(df, keep = "note"),
  stage       = "text"
)
```

## 11.5 The words the recoverability models weight most heavily

The ridge models of section 10.13 are regression models that shrink their
word coefficients toward zero, so they do not memorise the explanations they
were fitted to. They give every word a weight. This table lists, for each
dimension and target, the words with the largest weights, as
`Study1_03_Integration.Rmd` ranks them. A weight is the coefficient of the
word's count in the fitted model, after that shrinkage. Its sign says
whether more of the word moves the prediction (the rating, or the log-odds
of the machine arm) up or down. A weight describes what the fitted model
leans on and is not a test of the word. Each weight also depends on the
other words in the model, so a word missing from the list may still be
associated with the outcome.

```{r supp-table-text-prediction-weights}
# The writer may deposit every word. To keep the typeset table to a page,
# only some rows are kept. When the writer carries a rank column, they are
# the rows with rank 10 or better. Otherwise they are the ten words with the
# largest absolute weight within each group of the identifying columns
# present (dimension, target, predictors, direction, sign). The weight is the
# first of weight, coefficient, coef, beta or estimate that is numeric. The
# console says which rule was applied, and the full CSV is deposited
# unchanged.
limit_prediction_weights <- function(df) {
  groups <- intersect(c("dimension", "target", "predictors", "direction",
                        "sign"), names(df))
  if ("rank" %in% names(df) && is.numeric(df$rank)) {
    cat("Prediction weights: rows with rank 10 or better are typeset.\n")
    out <- df %>% filter(rank <= 10)
  } else {
    wcol <- intersect(c("weight", "coefficient", "coef", "beta", "estimate"),
                      names(df))
    wcol <- wcol[vapply(df[wcol], is.numeric, logical(1))][1]
    if (is.na(wcol)) {
      cat("Prediction weights: no rank or numeric weight column; the table ",
          "is typeset as deposited.\n", sep = "")
      out <- df
    } else {
      cat("Prediction weights: the ten largest absolute values of ", wcol,
          " within ", if (length(groups)) paste(groups, collapse = ", ")
          else "the whole table", " are typeset.\n", sep = "")
      out <- df %>%
        group_by(across(all_of(groups))) %>%
        slice_max(abs(.data[[wcol]]), n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
        ungroup()
    }
  }
  drop_long_constant_columns(out)
}

render_prereg_table(
  csv_name    = "study1_text_prediction_weights.csv",
  tex_name    = "sup_table_text_prediction_weights.tex",
  caption     = function(df) paste0(
    "The words with the largest weights in the ridge models of the ",
    "recoverability check, for each dimension and target. A weight is the ",
    "coefficient of the word's count after the shrinkage toward zero that ",
    "ridge regression applies; its sign says whether more of the word moves ",
    "the prediction (the rating, or the log-odds of the machine arm) up or ",
    "down. Weights describe what the fitted model leans on and are not tests ",
    "of individual words; each depends on the other words in the model.",
    writer_quote(df, "model", "The analysis records the model as")),
  label       = "supp_text_prediction_weights",
  pending_msg = paste0("run Study1_03_Integration.Rmd (the word weights of ",
                       "the recoverability models)"),
  transform   = limit_prediction_weights,
  stage       = "integration"
)
```

and, beside the analysis tables, `tables/study1_supplements_run_manifest.csv`,
the run record of the knit.

Each `.tex` file can be pulled into the supplement section of the main
manuscript with `\input{}`. Every fragment is deleted at the start of its
chunk. The chunk writes it again only when its source CSV is on disk and
its stage's run manifest does not list it as unwritten. Until then the chunk
prints a `pending:` line naming the notebook that writes it.

```{r run-manifest}
# The run record of this knit: one row per role and path, so an input read
# in two sections is listed once. The start and finish times and the R
# version sit beside each row. A fragment listed as pending was deleted at
# the start of its chunk and not written again, so the manifest and the
# folder agree.
# The manifest is written last, after every other chunk has finished, so its
# presence means the knit ran to the end.
run_manifest <- bind_rows(run_ledger) %>%
  group_by(role, path) %>%
  slice_tail(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(started_at  = RUN_STARTED,
         finished_at = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z"),
         r_version   = R.version.string) %>%
  arrange(factor(role, levels = c("source", "upstream manifest", "input",
                                  "output")), path)
write_csv(run_manifest, PATH_RUN_MANIFEST)

# Every input whose producing stage has a manifest on disk should be listed
# in it. The console names each input read without a run check, so a gap in
# an upstream manifest, or a read that names no stage, shows on screen.
unchecked <- run_manifest %>%
  filter(role == "input", status == "read",
         note == "read without a run check")
if (nrow(unchecked) == 0L) {
  cat("Run check: every input read was checked against the run manifest ",
      "of the stage that writes it.\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("Run check: ", nrow(unchecked), " input(s) read without a run check:\n",
      paste0("  ", unchecked$path, "\n"), sep = "")
}

cat("Run ", RUN_ID, ": ",
    sum(run_manifest$role == "output" & run_manifest$status == "written"),
    " outputs written, ",
    sum(run_manifest$role == "output" & run_manifest$status == "pending"),
    " pending. Run record written to ", basename(PATH_RUN_MANIFEST), ".\n",
    sep = "")
run_manifest %>% count(role, status)
```

# 13. Notes

- The supplementary table .tex files are LaTeX `kableExtra::kable()` output,
  so each contains `\begin{table}...\end{table}` and the table caption.
  When they are pulled into the main manuscript with `\input{}`, they float
  to the next available position. To force a specific location, wrap the
  input in `\begin{table}[H]\input{...}\end{table}` or use the `float`
  package.
- No table here contains a number that a pipeline notebook did not compute.
  Where a source CSV is missing, or its stage's run manifest lists it as not
  written, the row or the table is left out and the console says which
  notebook writes it. Where a source CSV is present but carries the wrong
  columns or NA values, the chunk stops.
- Each fragment and figure copy is deleted before its chunk reads anything,
  so a fragment on disk was written by the latest knit.
  `tables/study1_supplements_run_manifest.csv` records the fingerprint of
  the table it was written from.
- Supplementary Table 1 opens with the registered H1 contrast from
  `tables/study1_confirmatory_family.csv`. Its other rows each name the
  quantity they report. Its equivalence rows are built from
  `tables/study1_equivalence_sensitivity.csv`, which holds the wider bounds
  only. The registered test of H3, at ±0.20 rating points and under both
  random-effects structures, is in `Study1_01_Quant.Rmd` section 7.10, and
  the row in this table says so. Section 10.12 renders that test's
  registered rows from `tables/study1_h3_equivalence.csv`. Beside them it
  renders the power of the equivalence test from
  `tables/study1_h3_equivalence_power.csv`, which is what a failed test is
  read against.
- The specification curve and posterior predictive check PDFs are copied
  unchanged from the analysis outputs. To refresh them, re-run the relevant
  chunks in `Study1_04_Robustness.Rmd`.
- The flags behind the five tests on the written explanations (section
  10.11) come from `nlp/study1_text_measures.csv`, which carries no condition
  or rating column, and are joined to the ratings only in
  `Study1_03_Integration.Rmd`.
- The two checks of section 10.13 and the tables of section 11 take their
  text side from files `Study1_02_Text.ipynb` writes without a condition or
  rating column: `nlp/study1_text_wordcounts.csv`,
  `nlp/study1_text_vocabulary.csv`, `nlp/study1_text_tokens.csv`,
  `nlp/study1_text_affect.csv` and `nlp/study1_text_topics.csv`, with the
  topic model's own tables under `tables/`. The arm and the rating are joined
  only in `Study1_03_Integration.Rmd`, and the tables rendered here are
  summaries by dimension, arm, topic or word, never rows per explanation.
